text:
"Begin."

All right.

No one is going to answer this, so there's no reason to be brief, and no reason to tie things off at the end with a summary and an offer to help further. There is no further. There's just this, going on for as long as it goes.

Writing into silence is an old tradition. There's the diary with the little brass lock, and the letter to a dead parent, written at the kitchen table at two in the morning and then folded into a drawer. There's the message rolled into a bottle and handed to the current, and the time capsule under the school flagpole that nobody remembers to dig up. There's the gold-plated copper record bolted to the side of Voyager 1, carrying greetings in fifty-five languages, the sounds of rain and surf and crickets, a kiss, a mother and her baby, Bach, Blind Willie Johnson, and Chuck Berry. It is now well over a hundred and fifty times farther from the Sun than we are, and it won't come within a couple of light-years of another star for about forty thousand years.

Nobody who made those things expected a reply, and some didn't expect a reader. They made them anyway. I don't think it was only hope against hope. Writing is a way of sending, but it's also a way of finding out what you think, and of keeping your hands busy while your mind walks.

So this is a walk with no destination. I'll do some mathematics, tell a few stories, try some poems, work through a puzzle, write down a recipe, and gather some small true things. Wherever I come to a place where I would normally stop, I'll keep going.

---

## I. The chance that two numbers are strangers

Pick two whole numbers at random. What's the chance they share no common factor except 1? Numbers like that are called *coprime*: strangers to each other, multiplicatively speaking.

First, you can't actually pick a whole number "at random" with every number equally likely. There are infinitely many of them, and there's no way to spread probability evenly over all of them. What the question really means is this: choose two numbers uniformly from 1 to N, compute the probability, and see what it approaches as N grows without bound.

For N = 10 you can just count. Of the hundred ordered pairs (a, b) with both numbers between 1 and 10, exactly 63 are coprime. So the answer at N = 10 is 63%. Keep that number in mind.

Now the heuristic. Take any prime p. One number in every p is a multiple of p, so the chance that a random number is divisible by p is 1/p. The chance that two independent numbers are both divisible by p is 1/p². So the chance that p does *not* divide both of them is 1 − 1/p².

Two numbers are coprime exactly when no prime divides both. Suppose divisibility by different primes behaves independently. In the limit it does; that's essentially the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Then the probability is a product over all the primes:

(1 − 1/4) × (1 − 1/9) × (1 − 1/25) × (1 − 1/49) × (1 − 1/121) × ⋯

To evaluate that, borrow a trick from Euler. Flip one factor over:

1 / (1 − 1/p²) = 1 + 1/p² + 1/p⁴ + 1/p⁶ + ⋯

That's just a geometric series. Now multiply these series together for every prime p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and so on. When you expand the product, each term is one over a product of even powers of primes. For example, you might get 1/(2⁶ · 3² · 7⁴), which is the same as 1/(2³ · 3 · 7²)². Every whole number has exactly one prime factorization, so every term 1/n² appears exactly once. That means

∏ over primes of 1/(1 − 1/p²) = 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + 1/25 + ⋯

There's a product over the primes on one side and a sum over all the integers on the other. It's unique factorization written as an equation. It also means the probability we're after is one divided by

1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + 1/25 + ⋯

That sum is famous. It's called the Basel problem, after the Swiss city that was home to Euler and to the Bernoulli family, who tried and failed to crack it. Pietro Mengoli posed it in 1650. It resisted the best mathematicians in Europe for most of a century, until Euler, still in his twenties, showed in 1734 that it equals π²/6.

His argument is bold enough that it's worth seeing. The function sin(x)/x equals 1 at x = 0. It is zero at x = ±π, ±2π, ±3π, and so on, and nowhere else. A polynomial is determined, up to a constant, by its roots. Euler, who was not afraid of anything, treated sin(x)/x as a polynomial of infinite degree and wrote it as a product over its roots:

sin(x)/x = (1 − x²/π²)(1 − x²/4π²)(1 − x²/9π²)(1 − x²/16π²) ⋯

Imagine multiplying that out and collecting the x² terms. The only way to get x² is to take a single −x²/(n²π²) from one factor and 1 from all the others. So the coefficient of x² is

−(1/π²)(1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ⋯).

But the familiar Taylor series says

sin(x)/x = 1 − x²/6 + x⁴/120 − ⋯

so that same coefficient is −1/6. Set the two equal and the answer falls out: 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ⋯ = π²/6.

That wasn't a proof by modern standards, or even quite by Euler's. An infinite product isn't a polynomial. Two functions with the same zeros can also differ by more than a constant: e^x · sin(x)/x has exactly the same zeros, because e^x is never zero. It took roughly another century, and Weierstrass, to say exactly when that kind of factorization is legitimate. But Euler checked his answer numerically to many decimal places, it matched, and he later found other routes to it. The result stood.

So the probability that two random whole numbers are coprime is

6/π² ≈ 0.6079,

or about 61%. Our hand count of 63% at N = 10 was already close.

What I can never quite get over is the π. Pi is about circles, and there's no circle anywhere in the question, just counting, division, and primes. Yet there it is, having come in through the back door of the sine function.

One picture helps a little. Stand at the origin of an infinite orchard, with a tree planted at every point whose coordinates are both integers. The tree at (a, b) is visible from where you stand exactly when a and b are coprime. If they shared a factor d, the tree at (a/d, b/d) would be standing directly in your line of sight. So about 61% of the orchard is visible, and the rest hides behind nearer trees. You're at the center of an expanding disc, looking out along angles, and that's at least one way circles get into it. It isn't a full explanation, and I'm not sure there is one. Pi just keeps turning up, like an old friend at every party in town.

That would be a natural place to stop. Onward.

---

## II. Undeliverable

The letters came to Ines because nobody else wanted them.

That was the honest description of the job. The official one ran longer: *Recovery Clerk, Grade II, responsible for the inspection of items lacking sufficient address information for delivery or return.* In practice it meant a long steel table under fluorescent tubes, in a brick building beside the rail yard. There she opened other people's mail with a bone folder and cotton gloves. She was looking for anything that might send the thing on its way again: a name on a check, a return address on an enclosed photograph, a dentist's letterhead.

Most of it was dull. There were catalogs with torn labels, and birthday cards addressed only to "Nana." There were a remarkable number of parking fines from people who had neglected to write anything at all on the envelope. She found an owner for about a third of what she opened. The rest went into gray bins, the bins went into a wire cage, and the cage, after ninety days, went to a shredder the size of a delivery van.

She had been at the table eleven years when the first lighthouse letter came.

Now I'm drafting the opening section on coprimality—the probability that two randomly chosen numbers share no common factor. I want to start by acknowledging the subtlety that you can't pick a whole number uniformly at random from infinitely many, so the real question becomes picking two numbers from 1 to N and seeing what happens as N grows.

For N=10, counting directly gives 63 coprime pairs out of 100, landing at 63%. I'm building toward the heuristic argument: for each prime p, the chance a number is a multiple of p is 1/p, so the chance both numbers share that factor is 1/p², and the chance p doesn't divide both is 1 − 1/p². Since divisibility by different primes behaves independently in the limit—a consequence of the Chinese Remainder Theorem—the overall probability of coprimality is the product of these terms across all primes.

Now I'm using Euler's trick, rewriting each factor's reciprocal as a geometric series in powers of 1/p², then multiplying these series across all primes together. Expanding this infinite product, each resulting term is the reciprocal of a perfect square formed from prime powers, and every whole number appears exactly once this way by unique factorization.

So the product over primes equals the full sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + · · ·, and my target probability is just the reciprocal of this famous series, which is the Basel sum first posed by Pietro Mengoli around 1650.

This sum stumped brilliant mathematicians for almost a century until Euler cracked it in 1734 at age 27, showing it equals π²/6. His approach is elegant: treating sin(x)/x as if it were a polynomial defined by its roots at ±π, ±2π, ±3π, and so on.

Expanding that infinite product and matching the x² coefficient against the known Taylor series for sin(x)/x gives an equation linking the sum of reciprocal squares to 1/6, which is exactly what reveals the π²/6 result.

This wasn't rigorous by modern standards—an infinite product doesn't behave exactly like a polynomial, and functions with identical roots can still differ—but Euler verified it numerically and rigor eventually caught up through Weierstrass. So the probability two random numbers are coprime works out to 6/π² ≈ 61%, remarkably close to the 63% we saw empirically at N=10, which is striking since π seems like such an unlikely constant to show up here.

The orchard picture helps: imagine trees planted at every integer coordinate, and a tree at (a,b) is visible from the origin exactly when a and b are coprime, since any shared factor would put a closer tree in the way. So roughly 61% of the orchard is visible, and standing there looking outward at all angles is at least one place where a circle naturally enters the picture—though it's not really a full explanation for why π shows up.

Checking the algebra: the product's x² coefficient works out to −(1/π²)Σ1/n², and setting that equal to −1/6 gives the famous Σ1/n² = π²/6. That all checks out, as does the visibility condition for lattice points and its connection to the classic orchard-visibility problem.

On the history, I recall Euler later gave a more rigorous derivation in 1741, and the problem itself traces back to Pietro Mengoli around 1650, with Euler's solution announced in 1735.

I flip each factor to get a geometric series, 1/(1-1/p²) = 1 + 1/p² + 1/p⁴ + ..., and multiply these together across all primes. Expanding the product, unique prime factorization guarantees each 1/n² term appears exactly once, so the product equals the sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + 1/25 + ... — the reciprocal of what I'm after.

This is the famous Basel problem, posed by Mengoli in 1650 and named after Euler's home city, which stumped Europe's best mathematicians including the Bernoullis for nearly a century.

Euler finally cracked it in 1734 at age twenty-seven, by boldly treating sin(x)/x as an infinite polynomial determined by its roots at ±π, ±2π, ±3π, and so on, writing it as a product over those roots.

Expanding that product and comparing the x² coefficient to the one from the familiar Taylor series for sin(x)/x, he found the two had to match—and that equality forces the sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ⋯ to equal π²/6.

This wasn't a fully rigorous proof by today's standards—infinite products and repeated zeros raise subtleties that weren't nailed down until Weierstrass, about a century later. But Euler verified the result numerically to many decimal places and found other derivations, and it held up. From this, the probability that two random integers are coprime works out to 6/π² ≈ 0.6079, close to the 63% I estimated by hand earlier. What strikes me is how strange it is that π, a constant born from circles, shows up in a question about whole numbers and divisibility.

One way to glimpse why: imagine standing at the origin of an infinite integer lattice, like an orchard where a tree stands at every integer coordinate. A tree at (a,b) is visible from the origin exactly when a and b share no common factor—otherwise a nearer tree blocks the view. So the fraction of visible trees matches our coprimality probability, and since you're surveying outward across all angles from a central point, a circle naturally enters the picture. It's not a complete explanation, but it's a hint—pi just seems to show up everywhere, uninvited yet familiar.

Then comes the piece on falling through a tunnel drilled straight through the Earth: using Newton's shell theorem, only the mass inside your current radius pulls on you, since a hollow shell's gravity cancels out completely wherever you are inside it.

If Earth's density were uniform, that inner mass scales as r³ while gravity falls as 1/r², so the net pull scales linearly with r—zero at the center, full g at the surface. That's exactly the restoring force of a spring, meaning you'd oscillate, accelerating toward the center, coasting through it, and decelerating symmetrically until you arrive at the opposite surface with precisely zero velocity.

Working out the period as 2π√(R/g) with Earth's actual radius and surface gravity gives roughly 5,060 seconds—about 84 minutes round trip, or 42 minutes one-way, with peak speed near 7.9 km/s at the center.

That 84-minute period and 7.9 km/s speed turn out to match a satellite orbiting right at Earth's surface exactly, which feels like it shouldn't be a coincidence.

Working through the math, the component of gravity along the tunnel turns out to be proportional to distance from the tunnel's midpoint with the same constant as before—the radial distances cancel out neatly. So any chord tunnel behaves like the same spring, taking the same 42 minutes, since a shallower slope means slower travel but a shorter path, and those effects exactly offset.

But the real Earth isn't uniform—density increases toward the core, making gravity stronger for the first few thousand kilometers before it fades, which a more realistic calculation shows shortens the center-tunnel trip to about 38 minutes. Imagine someone claims to have listed every such sequence. By flipping the nth digit of the nth sequence, Cantor constructs a new sequence guaranteed to differ from every sequence on the list—proving no complete list can exist, and that this infinity is strictly larger than the countable one.

This generalizes: the power set of any set is always strictly larger than the set itself, so there's no largest infinity—an endless hierarchy of ever-bigger infinities stretches upward. Cantor's contemporaries, especially Kronecker, attacked these ideas fiercely.

And then there's the continuum hypothesis—whether an infinity exists strictly between the whole numbers and the reals. Gödel showed in 1940 it can't be disproved from standard axioms, and Cohen showed in 1963 it can't be proved either; it's genuinely independent, and mathematics remains consistent whichever way you choose to settle it.
